newsitem.title: USA: CIA chief says Koreas could be headed for war.
newsitem.headline: CIA chief says Koreas could be headed for war.

text.p: CIA Director John Deutch said on Wednesday that within three years North Korea would be headed for war with South Korea, collapse as a state or be on the road to reunification.
He told the Senate Intelligence Committee he considered it "uncertain" which way communist-ruled North Korea would go.

Relations between the North and the South have been in a deep freeze since Sept. 18, when a North Korean submarine went aground off the South carrying 26 commandos who went ashore. The two have faced each other across the world's most heavily fortified border since a truce ended the 1950-53 Korean war.

"Either it's going to ... invade the South over one issue or another -- war will break out. Or it will collapse internally or implode because of the incredible economic problems that the country faces. Or, third, it will over time lead to some peaceful resolution and reunification with the South," he testified in his final appearance before the panel.

"How that proceeds between those three directions will be resolved in the next two or three years. It is not something that will go on for decades," he said, adding that this was his own best "estimate."

A senior intelligence official, eager to avoid undue alarm, said later that Deutch had meant that North Korea's direction would be apparent within two or three years, "as opposed to one of those events will have occured."
President Bill Clinton has nominated his national security adviser, Anthony Lake, to replace Deutch as his third director of central intelligence.

But Committee Chairman Arlen Specter said he had "great reservations" about Lake because of his role in cutting Congress and the CIA out of a secret 1994 decision-making process on Iranian arms shipments to Bosnian Moslems.

As national security adviser, Lake was an architect of the policy that gave Croatia a secret green light to help ship the Iranian arms in violation of a United Nations embargo. The Senate committee, which is to hold the first vote on Lake, said in a recent report that he intentionally misled Congress and R. James Woolsey, Clinton's first CIA director.
In his testimony, Deutch said the intelligence community was gearing up for possible retaliation against attacks like the one that killed 19 Americans in Saudi Arabia in June.

Although he declined to discuss a possible response to the June 25 bombing of a U.S. military housing complex in Dhahran, he said U.S. intelligence agencies had been honing a covert action capability that Clinton could use to retaliate, preempt or disrupt "the activities and operations of world-wide terrorist organisations."

Deutch commented in reply to a question from Specter, who cited a Washington Post report on Wednesday that Saudi officials were trying to prepare the ground for possible multilateral retaliation against Iran early next year if Washington agrees that Iran was linked to the blast.
"I will say that the issue placed before me in your question I think regrettably is going to be progressively in front of the government in times to come," Deutch said.

Saudi Arabia has given the United States detailed data to support the Saudis' belief that the bombing of the Khobar Towers military complex was carried out by Shi'ite extremists trained in Lebanon and backed by Iran, the Post reported.

Deutch voiced satisfaction with a German murder case that some experts expect to implicate the Iranian government directly in assassination of overseas opponents. "I regard the German action as evidence of a greater appreciation of Iranian intentions and activities in sponsoring illegal activities and terrorist activities around the world," he said.
